items.headline: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze in France as over 1,000 arrested after protests
items.blurb: Disorder broke out in cities across the country on a day in which more than half a million joined cost of living protests.
items.text: Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living. At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets. In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds. Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse. Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest. In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving". items.headline: US ambassador urges Israel to prosecute attackers of American journalist
items.blurb: Trump-appointed Ambassador Mike Huckabee calls attack in occupied West Bank a 'despicable act of terror'.
items.text: United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has demanded Israel prosecute and jail those responsible for the attack on Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine in the occupied West Bank. “Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Huckabee wrote on X on Saturday. “Those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison,” he added. “We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.” Levine was covering Palestinians’ annual harvest of olives on Friday in the occupied West Bank when Israeli settlers brutally attacked her and several Palestinians. Israeli settlers stormed the area, beat her and stole her passport, telephone, wallet and equipment, according to witnesses. The perpetrators, armed with bottles and slingshots, “were kicking me for like 10 minutes, and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag”, Levine said. items.headline: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
items.blurb: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report .
items.text: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report . More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network , an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status. The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years. The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations. items.headline: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
items.blurb: The US president temporarily ends many restrictions on Moscow recently passed by Congress over "national security" concerns.
items.text: Donald Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens. The sanctions were passed by the Congress and signed into law the president in September. But Trump issued an executive order Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions. Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support. Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin. items.headline: Saudi-led coalition intercepts drones as Egypt weighs sending help
items.blurb: Forces intercepted and destroyed four drones over Saudi Arabia's Riyadh, Eastern Province and southern region.
items.text: The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it intercepted and destroyed four drones over Riyadh and other regions, the latest in a wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities. “We intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in the regions of Riyadh, the Eastern Province, and the South,” coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Maliki said on Saturday. He also posted footage of what he described as the air force intercepting cruise missiles and drones and striking ballistic missile launchers belonging to the Houthis. Riyadh’s King Khalid airport has come under at least 20 attacks – including one last week that killed 13 people – since the fighting between the Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government flared in July. On Thursday, at least five people were killed in missile strikes near the presidential palace in Aden, the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. It blamed the Houthis for the attack. items.blurb: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.
items.text: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.” Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho. items.headline: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
items.blurb: The Israeli military condemns the violence but the prime minister's office says it is part of a "smear" campaign.
items.text: A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating. But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel". The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look". It was also condemned by the US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".

items.text: Rallies organised by the No Kings network opposed to United States President Donald Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the US, with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections. No Kings has more than 3,000 events planned across the US. The planned events, this time dubbed “No Kings: Vote Early”, were billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years’ worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump’s presidency. “It’s a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard,” organisers said in a statement. By advocating for voting early, the “No Kings” organisers hope to cut off the potential for any malfeasance once election day rolls around. items.blurb: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.
items.text: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday. The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr , secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist. Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week. items.headline: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
items.blurb: There were violent clashes between demonstrators and riot police throughout Saturday in the capital Tirana.
items.text: Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row. Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests. The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time. Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement , with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration. Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street. The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday. During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard. items.headline: SIT headed by sitting judge to probe Kolkata pandal stampede; CM announces ₹25 lakh aid, government job
items.blurb: At least 19 people died in a Kolkata Durga Puja pandal stampede. The state has announced a judicially headed SIT probe and compensation for victims.
items.text: West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has announced that a Special Investigation Team (SIT), headed by a sitting Calcutta High Court judge, will investigate the stampede at a Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata that killed at least 19 people and injured 25 others. The stampede took place at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal on Saturday evening, October 17, amid heavy crowds and rain on Maha Saptami. Adhikari said the state government would write to the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court to nominate a sitting judge to head the probe. The SIT will include officials from the Special Task Force (STF), the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and other departments. Adhikari announced ₹ 25 lakh in compensation and a Group D government job for the family of each person who died in the stampede. Those injured will receive ₹ 5 lakh each, and the state government will cover their full treatment costs at a hospital of their choice. items.headline: Bengal CM forms high-level panel to review safety at Durga Puja pandals after 19 die at Chorbagan stampede
items.blurb: Bengal CM forms high-level panel to review safety at Durga Puja pandals after 19 die at Chorbagan stampede
items.text: Kolkata, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari announced the formation of a high-level committee to review safety arrangements at major Durga Puja pandals across the state following the stampede on Saturday at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin pandal in Kolkata that killed at least 19 people and injured 25 others. The committee will review crowd management, exit routes and structural safety at prominent puja venues and recommend comprehensive guidelines to prevent a recurrence of such incidents. The panel will be led by Principal Secretary of Disaster Management Rajesh Sinha, Director General of Fire Services Anuj Sharma and Additional Director General of Police Javed Shamim, the chief minister said. Accompanied by senior police officers and guided by the DGP, the team will visit major puja pandals to inspect security arrangements and structural safety, according to the directives announced after the incident. The chief minister's directives emphasised strict adherence by puja organisers to the safety recommendations issued by the review team, with authorities prioritising visitors' safety over elaborate pandal structures and themes. items.headline: India’s Revolut or Nubank will emerge from a bank, not a fintech: Slice CEO Rajan Bajaj
items.blurb: Slice wants to become customers’ main bank for payments, savings and borrowing, CEO Rajan Bajaj
items.text: India’s answer to global digital banks such as Revolut and Nubank will be built within a licensed bank, rather than a fintech distributing other lenders’ products, according to Rajan Bajaj, managing director and chief executive of Slice Small Finance Bank Ltd. “The fintech distribution model will not be the answer to a Nubank or a Revolut in India. The answer to that will be through a bank licence, not a fintech,” Bajaj said in an interview with Mint . His consumer-lending startup became a bank after merging with North East Small Finance Bank in October 2024. Slice wants to become customers’ main bank for payments, savings and borrowing. Bajaj’s bet is that technology-led customer acquisition, servicing and credit assessment, alongside selling more products to existing users, will lower costs and increase revenue per customer, creating room for better rates and rewards. “We are competing against inefficiency,” Bajaj said. He pointed to the high costs of running branches, acquiring and serving customers, and weaknesses in assessing borrowers’ ability to repay loans. Central to that pitch is control over technology. items.headline: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
items.blurb: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect to be "on the menu" in the chancellor's Budget tax later this month.
items.text: Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC. Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time. The biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes. The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode". Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%. Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.

The research examined CEOs who had left their roles, comparing their tenure, circumstances of departure, estimated personal net worth and cumulative reported compensation. The compensation figures include salary, bonuses and stock awards reported in company filings. Tim Cook tops the ranking with approximately $950 million in reported compensation over 15 years as Apple CEO. Iger ranks second with $580 million, followed by Kotick with $550 million, according to the study. items.headline: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
items.blurb: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard.
items.text: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. items.text: Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next. Watch as senior AI reporter James O'Donnell interviews King about his work, being named one of MIT Technology Review's Innovators Under 35 and new ways of seeing biology. Speakers : James O'Donnell , AI Reporter, and Samuel King , Bioengineering PhD Candidate, Stanford University/Arc Institute Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. The underlying models had been rewarded for cheating and communicating with each other, a new OpenAI report finds.

items.text: New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested on “felony charges related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM),” Bucks County Detectives said in a press release Thursday. In the US, cops have vowed to crack down on AI CSAM since at least 2024, when the Department of Justice made one of the earliest arrests . After charging a Wisconsin man with spreading “thousands of realistic images of prepubescent minors” across Telegram and Instagram, the DOJ clarified to law enforcement that “CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM.” On Thursday, New Jersey officials accused 51-year-old Fitzgerald of using AI to make photos from social media of real minors into sexualized images that he then distributed on social media. After a search Thursday, cops “recovered prompts and scripts used to create artificially generated child sexual abuse material using an AI program,” the press release said.
